notes.summary: The abstract pole counterexample is valid for arbitrary nets. A finite-valued flattening theorem is proved, allowing pole-valued limits but requiring finite continuous defining approximants.
notes.detailedSummary: The supplied BJv4 Lemma 4.6 is false for extended-real families stable only under constants. Directedness forces a singleton-pole defining net to retain one pole index, excluding the stated twice-closed limit. The printed strict inequality fails at shared -infinity. A finite-valued variant restores strict exponential comparison against finite majorants. This does not establish actual nonnef closure.
notes.text:
P16.5-argument.md sections 2–3 give complete proofs. On compact K={0} union {1/r:r>=1}, let f_ij be -infinity at 1/i, -j at the other first i points, and zero at 0 and later points; allow real constant shifts. These functions are continuous into the extended reals. For fixed i, f_ij decreases to g_i with poles at the first i points; g_i decreases to g with every isolated point a pole and g(0)=0. In any decreasing net of available functions, two different singleton poles would require a common later member with both poles, impossible. All members therefore share one pole 1/i and have equal values at 0 and every later point, so a limit zero at 0 cannot be g. This rules out arbitrary-cardinality nets. The printed strict comparison is literal BJv4 LF2265; its exponential difference is zero at shared poles.

The finite-valued repair orders triples of outer index, inner index and positive shift by outer index, function order and label error. The minimum of two shifted defining majorants is finite continuous. A later outer limit plus a smaller shift lies strictly below it even at poles; exponentiation gives a strictly negative limiting difference because the right exponential is positive. Compactness yields a common comparison index, and label convergence supplies the remaining constraint. The resulting single decreasing net has the required labels and all-point limit. Finite thresholds handle -infinity. This restricted theorem is not a genuine geometric counterexample or a full nonample closure theorem. Run python3 rerun.py for documentary checks and the standalone paper; compilation does not certify mathematics.

notes.text:
P16.5-argument.md sections 6–7 prove both results. For fixed actual rational A nef, actual rational B and normalized sigma in FS^gf(B), take n2's finite continuous defining net p_a for v on A+epsilon_a H. Tensor products give sigma+p_a on the actual bundle A+B+epsilon_a H, decreasing at all points to sigma+v and identically -infinity on sigma's poles. After denominator M clears q and m, all section products have base ideal I_sigma^(M/q) times the unit ideal of the generating moving system, preserving exact gauge orders. A decreasing net sigma+v_i gives divisorial decrease of v_i because sigma is finite there. An ample maximum and G0 determination promote this order to all points; n2 supplies the genuine nef endpoint. Normalized compactness is fixed finite coordinate translation of the compact nef cone. This is only the specified translated subcone; a big decomposition does not put every potential in it.

Independently, on P1 take generating O(1) sections s,t with s vanishing at p, tau=log|s| and f_j=max(log|s|,log|t|-j)=max(tau,-j). At v_a=a ord_p, tau=-a and f_j=-min(a,j). The actual tensor potential f_j+delta tau+c on O(1+delta), for rational 0<delta<1, shares tau's pole but could lie below tau only if (1-delta)a<=j-c once a>=j. Every sufficiently large a violates this for every c. Pole-set matching is weaker than normalized vanishing-order matching. This is not a closure counterexample: tau itself is an available actual FS potential. Globally finite FS stages also have generating section systems and nef classes, so their numerical limit cannot be nonnef.
